lead: An SCR, also called a thyristor or silicon controlled rectifier, is a four-layer P-N-P-N switch. With the anode negative it blocks in reverse whatever the gate does. With the anode positive it blocks until a small gate pulse starts conduction; then it latches on and the gate loses control. The latch works because two internal transistors feed each other. SCRs are used where a circuit must switch large AC or DC power slowly and reliably: controlled rectifiers, AC voltage controllers, battery chargers and HVDC links. This chapter explains the layers, the V-I curve and the two-transistor model that predicts turn-on.
prereq: You need: power diode blocking and conduction from Chapter 1.1, and the transistor current gain α.

blocks.text: An SCR is a single silicon crystal with four layers: P1, N1, P2 and N2. The outer P1 layer is the anode A. The outer N2 layer is the cathode K. The gate G is a metal contact on the inner P2 layer. Three PN junctions form between the layers: J1 at P1-N1, J2 at N1-P2, and J3 at P2-N2. Four layers give three junctions, but only three terminals come out: anode, cathode and gate.

With anode positive and cathode negative, J1 and J3 are forward biased, but J2 is reverse biased. J2 blocks current, so the SCR stays off. This is forward blocking. With anode negative, J1 and J3 are reverse biased and the SCR blocks in reverse. The gate contact injects a small current into P2. That current is the trigger; it does not carry the main load current.

sections.h3: V-I characteristics and the three regions

blocks.text: Plot anode-to-cathode voltage V_AK on the horizontal axis and anode current I_A on the vertical axis. In forward blocking, I_A is a small leakage current and the curve is nearly flat until V_BO, the forward breakover voltage. At V_BO, J2 avalanches and the SCR turns on even without gate current. A gate pulse turns it on earlier, at a lower V_AK.

After turn-on, the SCR enters forward conduction. The curve rises steeply at a low voltage drop, typically about 1 V to 2 V. The external circuit, not the SCR, sets the current. The gate can be removed and the SCR stays on because the two internal transistors now sustain each other.

Two current thresholds describe this latch. Latching current I_L is the minimum anode current just after turn-on that keeps the SCR on when the gate pulse ends. Holding current I_H is the minimum anode current that keeps an already conducting SCR on. I_L is larger than I_H. In reverse blocking, the curve shows only leakage until reverse breakdown, which is avoided.

sections.h3: Two-transistor model and the turn-on condition

blocks.text: Split the four layers into two transistors. T1 is PNP: emitter P1 (anode), base N1, collector P2. T2 is NPN: collector N1, base P2 (gate), emitter N2 (cathode). T1 collector connects to T2 base. T2 collector connects to T1 base. This closed loop gives regeneration.

Let α₁ = I_C1/I_A be the common-base current gain of T1, and α₂ = I_C2/I_K be that of T2. I_A is anode current; I_K is cathode current; I_G is gate current. KCL gives I_K = I_A + I_G. T1 collector current α₁I_A + I_CBO1 feeds T2 base. T2 collector current α₂I_K + I_CBO2 feeds T1 base. I_CBO1 and I_CBO2 are small leakage currents.

blocks.where: I_A is anode current in A; I_G is gate current in A; α₁ and α₂ are the common-base current gains of T1 and T2; I_CBO1 and I_CBO2 are the collector-base leakage currents in A.

blocks.text: When α₁+α₂ is well below 1, the denominator is positive and large. A small gate current produces only a small anode current. When α₁+α₂ approaches 1, the denominator approaches zero. The loop gain reaches one, each transistor drives the other harder, and anode current rises until the external circuit limits it. The SCR latches. A gate pulse only starts this process. After latch, gate current is not needed and cannot stop conduction.

figure.caption: Anode current enters PNP T1, its collector drives NPN T2, and T2 collector feeds back to T1 base. Gate current at T2 starts the loop; after latching the loop sustains itself.

spec.title: Two-transistor model
spec.aria: Anode current enters a PNP transistor, its collector drives an NPN transistor, and the NPN collector feeds back to the PNP base; gate current starts the loop.

examples.question: In the two-transistor model of an SCR, α₁ = 0.6 and α₂ = 0.3. Find α₁ + α₂. Can the SCR stay on after the gate pulse? Repeat if α₂ rises to 0.45.
steps: First case: α₁ + α₂ = 0.6 + 0.3 = 0.90. The loop gain is less than 1, so the regenerative action dies out. The SCR cannot stay on after the gate pulse; it returns to forward blocking.

Second case: replace α₂ by 0.45. α₁ + α₂ = 0.6 + 0.45 = 1.05. The loop gain reaches and slightly exceeds 1, so the two-transistor loop sustains conduction. The SCR stays on after the gate pulse, with current limited by the external circuit.
examples.answer: The sums are 0.90 (no latch) and 1.05 (latches); the SCR stays on only in the second case.
examples.check:
a1 = 0.6
a2_first = 0.3
a2_second = 0.45
print(round(a1 + a2_first, 2))
print(round(a1 + a2_second, 2))

traps: Gate current only starts conduction; it cannot turn off an SCR. Removing the gate pulse does not stop an on SCR; turn-off is commutation, covered later.
Latching current I_L is larger than holding current I_H. They are anode current thresholds at turn-on and turn-off, not gate ratings.
Do not confuse forward breakover voltage V_BO with reverse breakdown voltage. V_BO turns the SCR on without a gate; reverse breakdown damages the device.
In the two-transistor model, α₁+α₂=1 is the ideal turn-on boundary. Gate current starts the loop, but after latching the gate loses control.

quiz.q: Name the four layers of an SCR in order from anode to cathode, and name its three terminals.
quiz.a: P1, N1, P2, N2 from anode to cathode; terminals are anode A, cathode K and gate G.

quiz.q: Why does an SCR block current when its anode is positive but no gate pulse is applied?
quiz.a: Junctions J1 and J3 are forward biased but J2 is reverse biased. J2 blocks the main current, so only leakage flows.

quiz.q: For an SCR, α₁ = 0.5 and α₂ = 0.35. Find α₁ + α₂. Will it latch by the simple two-transistor condition?
quiz.a: 0.5 + 0.35 = 0.85, which is less than 1. The loop gain is below one, so it does not latch.

quiz.q: After an SCR latches, why does removing the gate pulse not turn it off?
quiz.a: T1 and T2 now supply each other's base current. The loop gain is at least about one, so conduction is self-sustaining and the gate is no longer needed. Turn-off needs anode current below holding current.

quiz.q: Define latching current I_L and holding current I_H. State which is larger.
quiz.a: I_L is the minimum anode current just after turn-on that keeps the SCR on when the gate pulse ends. I_H is the minimum anode current that keeps an already on SCR on. I_L > I_H.

quiz.q: What is breakover voltage V_BO, and how is it different from gate turn-on?
quiz.a: V_BO is the forward anode-cathode voltage at which J2 breaks down and the SCR turns on without gate current. Gate turn-on uses a gate pulse and can occur below V_BO.

quiz.q: An SCR has V_BO = 600 V. A gate pulse turns it on at V_AK = 200 V. Explain why this does not violate the meaning of V_BO.
quiz.a: V_BO is the no-gate breakover point. A gate pulse injects current into P2, raises the transistor loop gain, and lowers the voltage needed to latch. The device turns on below V_BO by gate control.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, phase-control thyristors are still built for thousands of amperes and kilovolts. HVDC line-commutated converters use them because they are robust and have low on-state loss. Research moves toward IGCTs, SiC and GaN for faster switching, but the SCR remains the reference device for very high power at line frequency. Search for phase control thyristor datasheet, SCR holding current latching current, and line-commutated converter HVDC.
